nameStory: The Ruff gets its name from the spectacular, fluffy collar of feathers that males grow during breeding season - like an Elizabethan courtier's ornate neck ruff! This dramatic plumage display transforms ordinary-looking shorebirds into flamboyant performers at their northern breeding grounds.
description: The Ruff is a medium-sized sandpiper that's quite rare in New England, with only 46 recorded observations. These European visitors are about robin-sized but with longer legs and bills typical of shorebirds. Males are notably larger than females and can look completely different depending on the season - from plain brown birds in fall to extravagantly plumed dancers in spring.

idTips.label: Size difference between sexes
idTips.description: Males are distinctly larger than females - almost like seeing two different species together, with males appearing bulkier and taller when feeding side by side

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Medium-length, straight bill that's darker at the tip and slightly drooped, feeling firm but flexible if handled during banding

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Orange, yellow, or greenish legs that look almost waxy in bright sunlight, varying between individuals

idTips.label: Breeding male plumage
idTips.description: Spectacular collar of long, loose feathers around the neck in spring, often multicolored and feeling soft and airy like down

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Shows thin white wing stripe and white patches on either side of the dark tail, creating a distinctive flashing pattern

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Probes methodically in mud with a steady, mechanical rhythm, often keeping its head down longer than other sandpipers

habitat: In New England, Ruffs turn up at muddy edges of inland ponds, flooded fields, and occasionally salt marshes during migration. They prefer shallow water with exposed mud where they can probe for invertebrates, often associating with other migrant shorebirds at prime stopover sites.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants may show up in late April through May, with males potentially showing partial breeding plumage and distinctive neck ruffs.
seasonality.summer: Extremely uncommon in summer, as most birds are on Arctic breeding grounds, though occasional non-breeding individuals might linger.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration time from July through September, when birds appear in plain brown plumage without the ornate breeding features.
seasonality.winter: Exceptionally rare in winter, as most birds winter in Africa and southern Europe rather than New England.

funFact: Male Ruffs are such elaborate performers that they actually set up "leks" - like avian dance clubs where multiple males gather to show off their wildly different colored ruffs and engage in choreographed battles, with some males even mimicking females to sneak matings!
confusionNotes: In fall plumage, Ruffs can be confused with Pectoral Sandpipers, but remember "Ruff and Ready" - Ruffs have that distinctive size difference between males and females and more upright posture when alert, while Pectoral Sandpipers are more uniformly sized.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this bird with the "rough" spelling - it's specifically named after the clothing accessory. Ruffs are primarily Old World birds, so any sighting in New England is noteworthy and should be reported to birding communities.
compareHints: Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers. They're larger than most of their cousins like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers, but smaller than Red Knots, with a more upright stance than the horizontal-feeding Sanderlings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
